title: L versus BPL
formal: Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, for every language \(S\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* decided with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by a uniform randomized Turing machine using \(O(\log (n+2))\) work space and polynomial time on inputs of length n, is there a uniform deterministic Turing machine deciding S with \(O(\log (n+2))\) work space?
definitions: The machines have a finite description, a read-only two-way input tape, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space counts all visited work-tape cells; the input tape is excluded. A randomized machine receives independent fair coin outcomes one at a time, without a freely rereadable random tape: an outcome must be stored in counted work space to be remembered. It halts with ACCEPT or REJECT on every input and every random tape within \(K(n+2)^{c}\) steps and uses at most \(K \log _{2}(n+2)\) work cells, for some constants K,c depending only on the machine. For each input x, acceptance probability is at least \(2/3\) if \(x\in S\) and at most \(1/3\) if \(x\notin S\). This is a language problem with no promise excluding intermediate-probability inputs. A deterministic decider must halt and give the correct answer on every input; any halting deterministic logarithmic-space decider has polynomially many configurations and hence polynomial running time. Both classes are uniform and have no advice. The deterministic machine and its space constant may depend on S. The equality does not demand a computable compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions, nor a particular pseudorandom-generator construction.

context_blocks.text: A logarithmic-space computation can maintain indices and counters while remembering only a small part of the input. Randomness lets it explore many possible choices without storing all of them. The equality asks whether this apparent extra power disappears when the required output is only a bounded-error decision about the input.

The memory convention is central. Fresh random outcomes can be read once; a machine cannot revisit an arbitrarily long random string without paying for its storage or reconstructing it. Conversely, the deterministic simulator is allowed a different constant in its logarithmic-space bound. The question concerns equality of language classes, not identical execution traces.

Saks and Zhou gave a deterministic simulation using \(O(\log ^{3/2} n)\) space. Hoza improved the bound to \(O(\log ^{3/2} n / \sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), with the expression understood asymptotically. These bounds are substantially below squared logarithmic space but remain above a constant multiple of log n.

The 2026 work of Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma improves error reduction for weighted pseudorandom generators. Its revised account distinguishes weighted generators from ordinary generators and attributes the relevant arity/error connection to Cheng and Hoza. Those parameter improvements do not establish the equality of classes asked here.

The catalogue separately contains a concrete optimal-generator problem for read-once branching programs. Such a construction can have consequences for logarithmic-space derandomization, but the language-class equality does not prescribe that particular construction. This completed card retains the original TCS-0026 identity and Wigderson reference while making the computation and error models explicit.

why: Determine whether randomness increases decision power when only logarithmic work space is available.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with the stated model, domains, promises and quantifiers. A conditional theorem settles only its conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof matching the full target.

importance.reason: A central derandomization question with a resource regime and known techniques distinct from P=BPP. Specialist work on space-bounded pseudorandomness, including 2026 weighted-generator results, documents continuing interest. The class equality merits a full card even alongside a more specific generator-construction target.

sentences: BPL permits bounded-error randomized decisions using logarithmic work space and polynomial time.
The question asks whether every such language has a deterministic logarithmic-space decider.
Random bits are fresh independent coin outcomes, and remembering them consumes counted work space.
Known deterministic simulations and recent weighted-generator improvements still use more space or establish different parameter guarantees.
The completed card keeps this class-equality target separate from constructing a particular optimal pseudorandom generator.
